title: Shared Gardens in Crowded Cities
instructions: Read the passage and choose the best answer according to the text.

paragraphs: In many crowded cities, residents live in flats with little or no private outdoor space. At the same time, unused pieces of land may remain between buildings or beside railway lines. Community gardens bring these two facts together. A local group receives permission to use a piece of land, divides it into smaller areas, and grows vegetables, fruit, or flowers. Although the gardens are usually small, their effects can reach beyond the food they produce.

One important benefit is social contact. City neighbours may live in the same building for years without speaking to one another. In a shared garden, people meet while watering plants, exchanging tools, or discussing what to grow next season. Older residents can pass practical knowledge to younger people, while newcomers can join an activity without needing perfect language skills. These repeated, informal meetings may create trust more naturally than an organised social event.

The gardens can also change how people think about food. Children who have only seen vegetables in shops learn that growing them requires time, weather, and care. Adults may try unfamiliar foods because another gardener offers them a small amount to taste. However, community gardens cannot supply all the food a neighbourhood needs. Their land is limited, and successful crops depend on local conditions. Their educational value may therefore be more important than the quantity they produce.

Running a shared garden is not always easy. Groups must decide who can use the land, how costs will be paid, and what happens when a member stops caring for a plot. Water can become a serious expense during a dry summer. There may also be disagreements about noise, compost, or the use of chemicals. Projects that survive usually have simple written rules and regular meetings where problems are discussed before they grow larger.

Local governments sometimes support gardens by lending public land or providing water tanks. This support is useful, but control should not move completely away from residents. People are more likely to care for a place when they help make decisions about it. A strong project therefore combines official support with local responsibility. Community gardens will not solve every environmental or social problem in a city, but they can turn an ignored space into a place that people value together over time.
